prompt: Every gang member wears a knitted balaclava covering the whole head, with no eye, nose or mouth holes; a large white ring is stitched round the face, and a red triangle sits high over the wearer's left eye (on the right of the picture, at about 2 o'clock); gloves on both hands, collars and cuffs closed, no skin showing anywhere. Five of them stand in a slack single-file queue across a cramped reception room in a tired British town-hall office at lunchtime, facing the counter as if their number is about to be called: one balaclava each in lime green, bubblegum pink, traffic-cone orange, cobalt blue and lemon yellow, worn with a shiny nylon tracksuit, a puffy supermarket anorak, a fleece zipped to the chin, and trainers on a speckled grey carpet. Behind the chipped beige laminate counter, where a bored desk would normally be, a tower of loose and bundled paperwork is wedged floor to ceiling and keeps going, punching up through a missing polystyrene ceiling tile beside a buzzing fluorescent panel; a single sheet of A4 in a curling plastic sleeve is sellotaped to its front, printed in bold black capitals: THE RULES. Around them the room is busy with small sad things: a red take-a-number dispenser on a pole, a rack of sun-bleached leaflets, a row of moulded orange plastic chairs bolted together, a dusty rubber plant, a wall clock, a hand-sanitiser station. Portrait frame, eye level, straight on from about four metres back with a wide 28mm-style lens, deep focus from the front of the queue to the paper, everything sharp. Lit by a single harsh flash fired from the camera into the midday room: flat frontal light, hard thin shadows hugging each figure and the counter edge, glossy hot spots on the laminate and the nylon, the background slightly darker than the subjects. Colour is loud and over-ripe, as on cheap colour negative film from a seaside snapshot, the masks fizzing against the nicotine beige walls and grey carpet. Nobody strikes a pose; they just wait. Deadpan, documentary, faintly ridiculous.
